- the field of study requirement is applicable depending on the level of study and when a student applies for their student permit.
- If the student applies for a study permit extension under the same program of study as the study permit they applied for before November 1, 2024, then they do not need to meet the field of study requirement.
- If the student applies for a study permit extension under a different program of study than the study permit they applied for before November 1, 2024, then their study permit extension application must meet the field of study requirements applicable to their study program to be eligible for a PGWP. Ifthe second program does not meet the field of study requirements, then the duration of the PGWP would be based on the duration of the PGWP-eligible program (i.e. the first program), and the applicant would have to apply for a PGWP within 180 days of receiving confirmation that they have completed the first program.
For more information, please see the following on PGWP instructions for clients: Work or live in Canada after you graduate-Canada.ca

To qualify for program stacking in relation to PGWP duration, both PGWP-eligible programs must be:
- a minimum of 8 months in duration; and
- completed at a PGWP-eligible DLI within 2 years of the completion of the first program
In determining whether a program is PGWP-eligible, the field of study requirement is applicable depending on the level of study and when a student applies for their student permit:
- If the student applies for a study permit extension under the same program for which they have study authorization via the study permit they applied for before November 1, 2024, then they do not need to meet the field of study requirement.
- If the student applies for a study permit extension under a different program from the one they were granted study authorization via the study permit they applied for before November 1, 2024, then their study permit extension application must meet the field of study requirements applicable to their study program to be eligible for a PGWP.

Q1: Regarding R220.1(1)(a): does a SP-holder become non-compliant under this particular provision if they had withdrawn
from their original DLI and switched to another one prior to November 8th?
A2: Under R220.1(1)(a), a study permit holder is considered compliant as long as they are actively pursuing their course or program of study at a designated learning institution (DLI). If a student withdrew from their original DLI and switched to another DLI prior to November 8th, they would not be non-compliant under this provision, as long as they followed the appropriate process for transferring between institutions and remained enrolled at the new DLI.
Q2: Regarding R220.1(1)(a) and (b): does a SP-holder become non-compliant under this section if they had withdrawn from their original DLI and did not enroll into any new studies?
A2: Under R220.1(1)(a) and (b), a study permit holder becomes non-compliant if they withdraw from their original DLI and do not enroll in any new studies. The conditions state that the permit holder must be enrolled at the designated learning institution named in their permit and actively pursue their course or program of study. If they withdraw and do not enroll in a new program, they are no longer meeting these conditions and are considered non-compliant.
Q3: Regarding R222(1)(a): did the SP become invalid on November 8th if the SP-holder had withdrawn from the original DLI and switched to another DLI prior to this date?
A3: Based on R222(1)(a), a study permit becomes invalid 90 days after the permit holder completes their studies or is no longer enrolled at the DLI named in the permit. The 90 days do not apply in this scenario as the student has withdrawn from their studies, rather than completing their studies. If a student withdrew from their original DLI and switched to another DLI before November 8th, 2024, the student should have changed DLI via their IRCC Account. However, if the student changed DLIs after November 8th, they will need to apply for a new study permit extension.
Q4: Regarding R222(1)(a): did the SP become invalid on November 8th if the SP-holder had withdrawn from the original DLI and had not enroll into any new studies prior to this date?
A4: Under R222(1)(a), if a study permit holder withdrew from their original DLI and did not enroll in any new studies, they are breaching the conditions of their study permit as they are not actively pursuing studies.

Under current instructions, a student on a leave from studies that was authorized by their designated learning institution (DLI), who did not resume their studies by the end of the authorized leave period, should either leave Canada, or change to visitor status or worker status. If their study permit will expire before they finish their courses, they must apply to extend their stay as a student before the expiry date. Students who submit the “Application to Change Conditions, Extend My Stay or Remain in Canada As a Student" form before the expiry date of the previous study permit will maintain their status as a temporary resident as per subsection R183(5). Under section R189, study permit holders may continue their studies if they have remained in Canada since the expiry of their study permit and continued to comply with the conditions, other than the expiry date, set out on the expired study permit. De : J> Envoyé : 16 octobre 2024 18:24 À : Objet : Permis de travail postdiplôme au Canada-admissibilité
Bonjour,
Je me présente,
Je voudrais signaler une contradiction entre le site web public d'IRCC et le bulletin opérationnel concernant l’admissibilité à la demande d'un permis de travail postdiplôme au Canada.
Sur le site public, section Diplômés de l’intérieur du Canada [https://www.canada.ca/fr/immigration-refugies-](https://www.canada.ca/fr/immigration-refugies-) citoyennete/services/etudier-canada/travail/apres-obtention-diplome/admissibilite.html l’on voit que les étudiants sont admissibles même s'ils sont en statut conservé (voir paragraphe surligné ne jaune)
Exigences d’admissibilité générales au PTPD
Vous pouvez demander un PTPD dans les cas suivants :
- avoir terminé un programme d’études dans un établissement d’enseignement désigné et répondre à certaines exigences du programme;
- avoir conservé le statut d’étudiant à temps plein au Canada, et ce, pour tous les trimestres de votre programme d’études; o Certaines exceptions s’appliquent à cette exigence, notamment
■ avoir étudié à temps partiel pendant votre dernier trimestre ■avoir pris un congé d’études autorisé; ■ avoir dû arrêter vos études ou passer à des études à temps partiel entre mars 2020 et le trimestre d’automne 2020 pour des raisons liées à la COVID-19;
- avoir obtenu un permis d’études ayant été valide au cours des 180 derniers jours
- avoir présenté une demande pour prolonger votre permis d’études avant l’expiration et aucune décision n’a été prise à l’égard de votre demande
Tandis que sur le site Permis de travail postdiplôme (PTPD) [R205c) - C43]- Programme de mobilité internationale-Canada.ca l’on voit que pour être admissible il faut absolument détenir un permis d’études valide.
Au Canada – permis d’études valide
Les permis d’études sont généralement délivrés pour 90 jours au-delà de la date de fin prévue du programme. Toutefois, les étudiants étrangers disposent de 180 jours à partir de la fin de leurs études pour présenter une demande de PTPD. Les demandeurs doivent conserver leur statut au Canada et leur capacité de présenter une demande depuis le Canada en vertu de l’article 199 du RIPR.
Les demandeurs peuvent présenter une demande de PTPD depuis le Canada si leur permis d’études est toujours valide (non expiré) ou s’ils satisfont à l’une des autres exigences énoncées à l’article 199 du RIPR au moment de présenter leur demande.
Conformément à l’alinéa 186w) du RIPR, le diplômé qui demande un permis de travail avant l’expiration de son permis d’études peut être autorisé à travailler sans permis de travail en attendant une décision relative à sa demande.
Important : Si un étranger a présenté une demande de prolongation de son permis d’études et qu’il étudie en vertu de l’article 189 du RIPR, l’article 199 ne s’applique pas à lui, et il doit attendre la réception de son nouveau permis d’études pour être
admissible en vertu de l’article 199.
Les délais de traitement des renouvellements de permis d'études ayant augmenté de manière exponentielle ces derniers mois, de nombreux étudiants finissants se retrouvent en statut conservé. Nous leur expliquons qu’ils doivent attendre que leur permis d'études soit approuvé avant de pouvoir déposer une demande de permis de travail postdiplôme au Canada, cependant les informations figurant sur le site web public les induisent en erreur.
Merci d'avance de l'attention que vous porterez à ce message.
Cordialement,

Distance learning
Distance learning can be through e-learning, correspondence, or Internet courses. Distance learning is a process by which technology is used in ways where the student does not have to physically be in the place where the teaching is taking place. Since by definition distance learning does not require one to be in Canada, a study permit cannot be issued for this type of course. For example, if a foreign national authorized to work in Canada is prohibited from engaging in studies as per a condition of their work permit, they are allowed to engage in distance learning courses. However, some distance learning courses include an in-Canada portion to the program (e.g., special tutorials or the writing of final exams). If the overall course of study is greater than six months, then the student requires a study permit for the in-Canada portion of the program, even if the in-Canada portion is less than six months. The duration of the study permit should be for the duration of the in-Canada portion only.

1. Foreign nationals may enter Canada or remain in Canada without a study permit to attend a course or program of study of 6 months’ duration or less [R188(1)(c)]. This exemption helps to facilitate access to short-term courses, regardless of their subject matter. The course or program of study may be part-time or full-time and should be completed within the period authorized upon entry (that is, up to 6 months). While a study permit is not required for short-term courses, an officer must accept and process an application for a study permit, even when the duration of the course or program of study is 6 months or less [R188(2)]. Holding a study permit for short-term courses may allow students to apply later, from within Canada [R215(1)(a)], to renew or change the conditions of their study permit for further studies. Study permit holders may also be eligible to participate in work programs that are available to international students [R186(f) and R205]. The duration of the course or program of study is often a more important consideration than the number of months the foreign national intends to study. With the exception of exchange programs, even if foreign nationals plan to study for 6 months or less, if the course or program is longer than 6 months, they need a study permit. While a foreign national may attend a short-term course or program without a study permit at a non-DLI, they may not be issued a study permit to attend courses at a non-DLI [R216(e)]. Additionally, please note that as of June 27, 2023, a temporary public policy allows eligible foreign workers to study without a study permit. For more information, please consult our website: Public policy allowing some work permit holders to study without a study permit-Canada.ca.
For more information, please consult our website: Study permits: Who needs a study permit-Canada.ca.

Merci pour votre réponse. Je souhaite préciser davantage ma demande initiale afin d’apporter plus de clarté à la situation.
1. Un Permis de séjour temporaire (PST)
2. Une fiche de visiteur, dont la durée de validité est alignée sur celle du PST.
Depuis son arrivée au Canada, cet enfant a obtenu un passeport ukrainien valide, ce qui élimine les motifs d’inadmissibilité ayant initialement justifié l’octroi du PST.
Actuellement, l’enfant souhaite prolonger son séjour au Canada et obtenir soit un permis de travail ouvert, soit un permis d’études.
Cependant, dans la pratique, les clients dans une situation similaire, titulaires d’un PST et d’un autre permis (soit d’études, soit de travail), voient systématiquement leurs demandes de changement de statut refusées. Les agents justifient ces refus en indiquant que le demandeur doit soumettre une nouvelle demande de PST, ce qui est incohérent puisque l’enfant possède désormais un passeport valide et n’est plus inadmissible.
Ainsi, selon ma compréhension de la situation actuelle, il est impossible de changer un PST vers un autre statut temporaire (par exemple, celui d’étudiant ou de travailleur) tout en restant au Canada. La seule option prévue dans la loi serait de quitter le Canada pour mettre fin au PST. Toutefois, cette solution n’est pas réalisable, car l’enfant ne dispose pas d’un visa de résident temporaire (VRT) apposé dans son passeport, ce qui rend tout retour impossible après son départ.
Je souhaite donc obtenir des précisions sur la procédure à suivre pour prolonger son statut temporaire en tant qu'étudiant ou travailleur, compte tenu du fait qu’il détient simultanément un PST et une fiche de visiteur, et qu’il n’existe pas de motifs valables pour demander un nouveau PST sans quitter le pays.
Cette problématique est fréquente parmi les personnes ukrainiennes arrivées au Canada sans passeport mais en ayant obtenu un sur place.
Je reste à votre disposition pour tout renseignement complémentaire et vous remercie pour votre assistance.
Cordialement,
Bonjour
Merci d’avoir joint les services d’IRCC.
Dans le cadre des mesures d’immigration et de soutien pour les Ukrainiens et les membres de leur familles, les ressortissants ukrainiens et les membres de leur famille qui détiennent un visa de résident temporaire (VRT) ou un permis de séjour temporaire (PST) délivré à la suite des mesures de facilitation dans le cadre de l’Autorisation de voyage d’urgence Canada-Ukraine (AVUCU), qui sont arrivés au Canada dans le cadre de l’AVUCU au plus tard le 31 mars 2024 et qui détiennent un statut de résident temporaire valide sont admissibles à un accès facilité à un nouveau permis d’études, à un nouveau permis de travail ouvert ou au renouvellement d’un permis de travail. Les titulaires de PST ont un statut de résident temporaire.
Les clients admissibles à ces mesures peuvent demander un nouveau permis de travail ouvert, le renouvellement de leur permis de travail ouvert actuel ou un nouveau permis d’études même si leur statut n’expire pas au cours de l’année suivante, à condition qu’ils présentent une demande avant le 31 mars 2025. La période de validité du permis de travail ouvert est soumise à la validité du passeport du client, ainsi qu’à la discrétion de l’agent de traitement, mais peut aller jusqu’à trois ans. Ces demandes sont assujetties aux frais réguliers.
Les clients qui désirent prolonger leur séjour à titre de visiteur peuvent présenter une demande selon le processus régulier : Prolonger votre séjour au Canada.
\cbpat8\sb280\fOUne fiche du visiteur indique que le client a le statut de visiteur au Canada ainsi que la durée maximale de leur séjour. Il ne garantit pas que le client peut quitter le Canada puis y revenir. Un ressortissant ukrainien doit avoir un visa de visiteur valide chaque fois qu’il veut entrer au Canada, sauf s’il revient directement d’un séjour aux États-Unis ou à Saint-Pierre et Miquelon. Si le client n’a pas de visa de visiteur valide apposé à leur passeport, il doit présenter une demande en fonction de leur situation : Résidents temporaires qui voyagent à l’extérieur du Canada : ce qu’il vous faut pour entrer de nouveau au Canada.
\sb173Veuillez vous référer aux Mesures d’immigration et de soutien pour les Ukrainiens et les membres de leur famille pour plus de détails.
Cordialement,

Cette demande concerne notamment un cas spécifique, mais reflète également des situations similaires auxquelles de nombreuses personnes ukrainiennes se retrouvent confrontées.

2. Une fiche de visiteur (Visitor Record) ayant la même durée de validité que le TRP.
Depuis son entrée au Canada, l’enfant a obtenu un passeport ukrainien valide et souhaite poursuivre son séjour au Canada pour étudier ou travailler. Toutefois, cette situation présente plusieurs obstacles :

Cette situation requiert une réponse rapide, car sans régularisation, leur statut temporaire au Canada pourrait être compromis, ce qui risquerait également d’affecter leurs démarches futures d’immigration, notamment celles visant l’obtention du statut de résident permanent.
Par ailleurs, la guerre en Ukraine continue de s’aggraver chaque jour, rendant cette régularisation d’autant plus cruciale. Une solution rapide et adaptée est essentielle pour assurer leur sécurité et leur avenir au Canada.

RESPONSE : The following guidelines are used to assess an applicant's PGWP eligibility when the applicant has taken courses by distance learning in Canada at an eligible DLI:
- If more than 50% of the program of study's total courses are completed by distance learning, the program may reasonably be considered a distance-learning program, and the applicant is ineligible for a PGWP.

In general, for PGWP eligibility in relation to distance learning, the applicant must have completed the majority of their studies in Canada, unless special measures apply to their situation. For example, if an applicant worked for an employer for 11 months on an open post-graduate work permit, and then for one month on an LMIA-exempt, employer specific work permit as free trade agreement professional for that same employer, would this be sufficient for obtaining points for an LMIA-exempt job offer assuming all other requirements are met?
threads.answer:
Yes, the applicant can count the 11 months on an open PGWP and the one month on the LMIA-exempt towards their one year of work experience for arranged employment. To obtain the points for arranged employment under 29 of the Ministerial Instructions respecting the Express Entry System, the applicant must have gained the work experience under the same employer, however there is no specification this work experience must be gained with an employer specific work permit, so that points would be granted. The work experience must still meet the requirements of the program. The applicant must still hold a valid work permit issued under the circumstances described in paragraph 204(a) or (c) or section 205 of the Regulations.

Family members can be added to the application at any time during the process, including after the visa is issued, but prior to obtaining permanent resident status.

The Federal Skilled Worker program and the Category- based selection rounds require that qualifying work experience is obtained during continuous employment to be eligible towards the minimum selection criteria. The continuous requirement applies both to full-time work and its part-time equivalent. It is meant to make periodic, intermittent, seasonal, infrequent, or brief employment ineligible for the minimum selection criteria under these programs. Vacation periods, regular sick leave and other standard paid leave entitlements as provided for in collective agreements, workplace legislation and/or individual employer policies are not necessarily considered interruptions in continuous

« Exigences d’admissibilité générales au PTPD
Vous pouvez demander un PTPD dans les cas suivants :
- avoir terminé un programme d’études dans un établissement d’enseignement désigné et répondre à certaines exigences du programme;
- avoir conservé le statut d’étudiant à temps plein au Canada, et ce, pour tous les trimestres de votre programme d’études; o Certaines exceptions s’appliquent à cette exigence, notamment
■ avoir étudié à temps partiel pendant votre dernier trimestre avoir pris un congé d’études autorisé; ■ avoir dû arrêter vos études ou passer à des études à temps partiel entre mars 2020 et le trimestre d’automne 2020 pour des raisons liées à la COVID-19;
- avoir obtenu un permis d’études ayant été valide au cours des 180 derniers jours
- avoir présenté une demande pour prolonger votre permis d’études avant l’expiration et aucune décision n’a été prise à l’égard de votre demande »

« Au Canada – permis d’études valide
Les permis d’études sont généralement délivrés pour 90 jours au-delà de la date de fin prévue du programme. Toutefois, les étudiants étrangers disposent de 180 jours à partir de la fin de leurs études pour présenter une demande de PTPD. Les demandeurs doivent conserver leur statut au Canada et leur capacité de présenter une demande depuis le Canada en vertu de l'article 199 du RIPR.

demande.

Les étrangers peuvent présenter une demande de permis de travail postdiplôme (PTPD) :
- * soit au Canada, s’ils sont admissibles (article 199 du RIPR); ou
- * à l’extérieur du Canada (article 197 du RIPR).
Les demandeurs éligibles peuvent présenter une demande pour le PTPD à un moment donné au cours des 180 jours suivant l’obtention de leur diplôme.
- * Les demandeurs qui ne peuvent plus demander de permis de travail au Canada au titre de l’article 199 du RIPR peuvent soumettre leur demande électroniquement afin qu’elle soit traitée à l’extérieur du Canada au titre de l’article 197 du RiPR. Ils peuvent demeurer au Canada tant qu’ils conservent leur statut de résident temporaire, ou ils peuvent quitter le Canada et attendre qu'une décision soit prise concernant leur demande de PTPD.
- * Les étudiants qui ont terminé leur programme d’études au Canada peuvent également quitter le pays et demander leur PTPD depuis l’étranger.
Veuillez noter que les étudiants peuvent travailler à temps plein jusqu'à ce qu’une décision soir prise à l’égard de leur demande de permis de travail dans les situations suivantes :
- * ils avaient un permis d'études valide au moment où ils ont soumis leur demande;
- * ils ont terminé leur programme d’études;
- * ils avaient le droit de travailler hors campus sans détenir de permis de travail pendant leurs études et ils n’ont pas travaillé un plus grand nombre d’heures que celui auquel ils avaient droit.
Vous trouverez plus d’informations sur les sites Web suivants :

Nous espérons que ces informations vous seront utiles.
Cordialement,

Je vous écris pour solliciter des précisions quant au processus de demande du permis de travail post-diplôme (PTPD) dans le cas d'un étudiant dont le permis d'études arrivait à expiration pendant l'attente des documents de graduation. Afin de maintenir son statut légal au Canada, une fiche de visiteur a été demandée avant l'expiration du permis d'études.
Conformément aux directives de votre site, il semble qu'un statut d’étudiant valide soit nécessaire pour pouvoir déposer une demande de PGwP. Dans cette situation, pourriez-vous confirmer si le rétablissement du statut d’étudiant est requis pour ensuite faire la demande de PTPD ?
and Cizenship Canada et Coyenneté Canada
Diplômés de l'intérieur du Canada Vous pouvez présenter une demande si vous réunissez tous les autres critères d’admissibilité et si vous êtes un diplômé résidant au Canada.
Ne laissez pas votre statut expirer en attendant votre relevé de notes.
Si votre permis d'études expire avant l’obtention de vos notes, vous avez deux options. Vous pouvez soit :
- présenter une demande de fiche du visiteur pour rester plus longtemps au Canada;
- quitter le Canada et présenter votre demande de PTPD.
Si vous restez au Canada et laissez votre permis d'études expirer, vous devez présenter une demande pour rétablir votre statut d’étudiant en vue de demander votre PTPD. Pour rétablir votre statut, vous devez payer des frais supplémentaires. Une autre option envisagée serait de soumettre la demande de PTPD depuis l’extérieur du Canada. Dans ce cas, est-il également indispensable de demander un permis d’études au préalable ? L'étudiant doit-il impérativement quitter le pays ou peut-il faire la demande depuis l’étranger tout en restant au Canada en tant que visiteur ? Diplômés de l’extérieur du Canada
Pour présenter une demande de PTPD en tant que diplômé à l'extérieur du Canada, vous devez réunir tous les autres critères d’admissibilité et les exigences suivantes :
- Vous disposez d’un permis d’études valide •Vous étiez inscrit à un programme en cours en mars 2020 ou
- Vous avez entamé un programme entre le printemps 2020 et l'été 2022 et vous avez un permis d’études; o votre demande de permis d'études a été approuvée; ou ovous avez demandé un permis d’études avant d’entamer votre programme d’études; votre permis d'études doit éventuellement être approuvé.
Seule la période que vous avez passée à étudier à l’extérieur du Canada après que nous avons reçu votre demande de permis d’études compte dans la durée de votre PTPD.
Si vous avez terminé votre programme d’études au Canada, vous pouvez également quitter le pays et demander votre PTPD depuis l'étranger.
Enfin, nous aimerions également confirmer que le délai de 180 jours pour présenter la demande de PTPD commence à courir à partir de la date officielle de graduation. Comme cet étudiant n’a pas encore été officiellement diplômé, ces 180 jours n’ont-ils donc pas encore commencé à compter?
Nous vous remercions par avance pour votre aide et vos éclaircissements sur ce dossier.
Cordialement,

Dear ImmReps,
I am seeking clarity regarding whether Provincial Attestation Letters (PALs") are required for existing study permit holders who apply for changes in conditions (e.g. to attend a new DLI). This seems to be inconsistent with the legal basis for PALs as follows:
1. As far as I’m aware, PAL is a creature of MI 70. The MI sets out its scope as: These Instructions apply to applications for a study permit made under the student class, referred to in Part 12 of the Regulations, except for:
a. study permit applications referred to in subsection 215(1) of the Regulations;
b. study permit applications referred to in subsection 215(2) of the Regulations;
c. study permit applications from foreign nationals planning to study at the primary school or secondary school level; or
d. study permit applications from foreign nationals planning to study in a graduate degree program at the master's or doctorate level.
The MI, and therefore the PAL requirement, is not applicable to situations covered by IRPR 215(1) and (2) which basically involve all permitted SP applications from within Canada. This would include applications by existing SP holders whether for extensions or otherwise.
2. Students who change institutions after beginning study in Canada would presumably fall under IRPR 215(1). Of course, if their SP expires or is invalidated due to non-enrolment under IRPR 222(1)(a.1), then that would no longer bring them under IRPR 215(1), but let’s assume their SP is valid when they apply for a new SP.
3. The application for a new SP within Canada to attend another DLI would presumably be for a “change of conditions" and not necessarily an extension.
4. IRCC guidance regarding PALs indicates that the PAL 215(1) exemption is for extensions (somewhat unclearly, but the reference to extensions only is there). However, this distinction seems to only be made in the IRCC guidance and not in either MI 70 or IRPR 215(1). I wonder, therefore, how requiring a PAL for a valid SP holder applying for a SP within Canada for a new DLI would be supported in law?
Thank you
Kind regards,

threads.subject: Examining permanent residents at a POE-REP-2024-2611 - Due 13-Jan-25
threads.answer:
Good morning,
As stated on our website, commercial transporters are legally required to ensure passengers are properly documented for travel to Canada. Section 148 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) outlines the obligations of commercial carriers and section 259 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) lists the prescribed documents that a person requires to enter Canada. A permanent resident (PR) that does not hold any of the prescribed documents outlined in section 259 of the IRPR should not be permitted to board a commercial carrier. Expired PR cards, Confirmation of Permanent Residence (CoPR) documents, and Records ofLanding (IMM 1000) are not valid for travel to Canada, but may indicate that a client held PR status at one point in time.
Section 11.3 of ENF 4 outlines the procedures for examining PRs at ports of entry (POEs). If a PR arrives at the POE without a valid PR card or PRTD, BSOs must first determine whether the person is a PR. When documentary evidence is not available, BSOs will refer the client for an Immigration examination to ask them questions about their identity and to check their status in the Global Case Management System (GCMS). The person is considered a foreign national until the BSO is satisfied that the person is a PR. The burden of proof lies on the person who is claiming to be a PR at a POE.
Paragraph 19(2) ofIRPA gives PRs the right to enter Canada once it is established that a person is a PR; however, as per paragraph 27(1) of IRPA, this right to enter and remain in Canada is subject to the provisions of the Act, and does not preclude the CBSA from ensuring that PRs are in compliance with IRPA and thus admissible to Canada. If the BSO believes that the PR is not in compliance with the residency obligation, they are to explain that while it has been established that they have a right to enter Canada, there is some reason to believe they could be the subject of a report under IRPA which could lead to the issuance of a removal order. If the BSO believes on a balance of probabilities that the PR has failed to comply with the residency obligation and there is sufficient evidence at the time of the examination to support the allegation, they may report the person (pursuant to A44(1)). If the PR refuses to provide any further information and enters Canada and where there is not sufficient evidence to support the writing of an inadmissibility report, the BSO may forward any available information to an inland office who will then determine whether an investigation is warranted.
Thank you,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox
De :1 Envoyé : 13 décembre 2024 14:54 À : Objet : RE: Examining permanent residents at a POE
Dear IRCC,
I would like clarification regarding the examination of permanent residents at a POE and their admission to Canada.
As per Section 7.8 of ENF Manual 23 - Examining permanent residents at a POE (enf23-eng.pdf):
When a permanent resident appears at a POE for examination, the officer must confirm that the person is a permanent resident. Officers must remain cognizant of the fact that the Act gives permanent residents of Canada the right to enter Canada at a port of entry once it is established that a person is a permanent resident, regardless of non-compliance with the residency obligation in A28 or the presence of other grounds of inadmissibility.
Port of entry (POE) officers can refuse entry to a permanent resident only when the person has already lost the status in accordance with the provisions of A46 (such as when a final determination has been made that they have failed to comply with the residency obligations or when a removal order comes into force). In other words, once a permanent resident's status is established, the person may enter Canada by right and the immigration examination under IRPA concludes.
According to the IRCC website ([https://ircc.canada.ca/english/helpcentre/answer.asp?qnum=064&top=10](https://ircc.canada.ca/english/helpcentre/answer.asp?qnum=064&top=10)):
You need a valid permanent resident (PR) card to return to Canada by plane, train, bus or boat.
If you try to return to Canada without a PR card or PRTD, you may not be able to take your flight, train, bus or boat to Canada.
My question is as follows:
Suppose that a permanent resident, who is outside of Canada and not in possession of a valid PR Card or PRTD, but who does have other proof of permanent residence (such as an expired PR Card, COPR or IMM 1000), and who nonetheless travels to Canada by commericial carrier and presents themselves at a POE with proof of their permanent residence. In such a situtation, is the officer required to make a determination as to whether or not that person is in fact a permanent resident (regardless of non-compliance with the residency obligation)? If the answer to this question is yes, then my subsequent question is (1) is the officer required to admit that permanent resident to Canada and (2) is the officer required and/or does the officer have the discretion to assess whether or not that person is in compliance with their residency obligation?
Respectfully yours,
and Citizenship Caneda

Please note that this mailbox is intended for general guidance and does not provide responses to case-specific inquiries. If you have case specific questions about a file, you are encouraged to submit a Webform at: [http://www.ircc.canada.ca/english/contacts/web-form.asp](http://www.ircc.canada.ca/english/contacts/web-form.asp)
Family Class
There are two processes that must be completed for international adoptions: the adoption process and the immigration process.
Adoptions are the jurisdiction of the Canadian provinces and territories. For the immigration process, applications to sponsor a child to be adopted in Canada must meet the requirements under R117(1)(g)
For more information on domestic or intercountry adoption, please refer your client to contact the provincial or territorial authority for adoption where they live, who will guide them through the adoption process and requirements and answer any questions they may have. Please refer your client to the following link to find their provincial or territorial adoption authority: Adoption authorities-Canada.ca.
Humanitarian and Compassionate (H&C) Considerations
Foreign nationals who are inadmissible or who do not meet the requirements ofthe Immigration and Refugee Protection Act or Regulations may make a written request for Humanitarian and Compassionate consideration under subsection A25(1).
Humanitarian and compassionate (H&C) consideration: Intake and who may apply-Canada.ca
Permanent resident visa applicants who do not meet the applicable criteria or obligations ofthe inmigration class they are applying under and wish for H&C grounds to be considered must provide additional written information in support of their request for consideration under subsection A25(1) (H&C considerations). This must be included as part of their immigration application under the family class, economic class, or refugee class. Applicants are free to make submissions on any aspect of
and Citizenship Caneda
their personal circumstances that they believe are relevant to their request for H&C consideration. The applicant bears the onus of satisfying the decision maker that the H&C factors and their individual circumstances are sufficient to warrant the exemption(s) requested. Requests for H&C consideration are reviewed on a case-by-case basis. The H&C decision-making process is highly discretionary. The decision maker considers whether a special grant of an exemption from the requirements of the Act is warranted. Invoking sections A25(1) and A25.1 is an exceptional measure and not simply an alternate means of applying for permanent resident status in Canada.
It is important to note that only foreign nationals may put forth H&C requests.
If a positive H&C decision is made, the applicant must still satisfy the remaining requirements for permanent resident visas including medical, criminal records checks and security screening. Once all requirements are met, a permanent resident visa may be issued.
The guide (IMM 5196) for sponsorship of adopted children and other relatives indicates that applications must be submitted electronically.
The sponsor is unable to request H&C for a sponsorship application (IMM1344), however, they are able to indicate on the IMM1 344 form that they wish to continue processing if they don't qualify as a sponsor, so that the applicant's H&C request may be examined.
If you have any further questions, we recommend submitting your inquiries through IRCC's web form: IRCC Web form-Canada.ca
For more specific advice you may want to consult an immigration lawyer.
Thank you,

threads.subject: Clarification on PGWP Eligibility for Study Permit Extensions-REP-2024-2414 - Due 24-Dec-24
threads.question: I am seeking clarification regarding the newly implemented rules on Post-Graduation Work Permit (PGWP) eligibility. According to the updated guidelines: f0"If you submitted your study permit application on or after November 1, 2024, you must have graduated from an eligible field of study." My question concerns in-Canada extensions for students continuing in the same institution or program. For example: If a student initially received their study permit before November 1, 2024, but reduced their course load and now requires an extension, will they still need to meet the new eligibility criteria?
threads.answer:
If the student applies for a study permit extension under the same program of study as the study permit they applied for before November 1, 2024, then they do not need to meet the field of study requirement.
If the student applies for a study permit extension under a different program of study than the study permit they applied for before November 1, 2024, then their study permit extension application must meet the field of study requirements applicable to their study program to be eligible for a PGWP. Please note that all PGWP applications (except those from flight school graduates) submitted on or after November 1, 2024 must comply with the new language requirements, regardless of when the student applied for their study permit or when they started their program of study. We are in the process of updating the program manual instructions, in the meantime we have recently updated our website to provide clients with further details on the new PGWP eligibility requirements at the following link: Work in Canada after you graduate: Who can apply-Canada.ca

- Toutefois, si un demandeur présente une demande de prolongation de permis d’études le 1er novembre 2024 ou après cette date, dans le cadre d’un programme d’études différent de celui pour lequel il a demandé le permis d’études avant le 1er novembre 2024, sa demande de prolongation de permis d’études doit satisfaire aux exigences relatives au domaine d’études pour être admissible à un PTPD.

Question:
QUESTION: LAW –IRPR s.209.3(1)(a)(xiii) The employer is required to obtain and pay for private health insurance during the "period of employment” to ensure that the employee has emergency medical care for the FN, for “...any period during which the foreign national is not covered by the provincial or territorial health insurance system".
When does the “period of employment" begin?
For example, a FN arrives in Canada on August 1st, 2024 and is granted an employer specific work permit at the border, but their contract of employment has an official start date of August 15th, 2024. Does the period of employment begin on the date of arrival or their first day of work (as stated in the contract of employment)?
Response:
The “period of employment” generally begins on the start date specified in the employment contract between the employer and the foreign national (FN), as this date reflects when the FN expected to begin fulfilling their work duties.
While the work permit authorizes the foreign national to begin work upon arrival, the start date in the employment contract typically determines the formal beginning of the “period of employment." Employers are still res ponsible for providing private health insurance from the foreign national arrival date to cover any gap before they qualify for provincial or territorial health coverage. This ensures compliance with IRPR s. 209.3(1)(a)(xiii) and protects the FN during any waiting period for provincial or territorial health insurance eligibility.
Additionally, it is important to note that employer compliance inspections may be conducted to ensure adherence to all regulatory obligations. Staying compliant not only protects the rights of the foreign national but also helps employers avoid potential issues in the future.
For more information on employer compliance, please visit Employer compliance inspections-Canada.ca
Thank you.

Students who have already changed DLIs before November 8 and who have already started their programs at the new DLI should have submitted their DLI transfer information in their online account as per the instructions in effect before the regulation changes. However, because these students have already started their program at the new DLI prior to the November 8 regulations changes, no further actions are necessary on their part, and they can continue studying as long as their current study permit is valid. If these students make subsequent DLI changes, they will need to apply for a new study permit extension as per the new regulations that came into force on November 8, 2024.

threads.answer:
Bonjour Mariana,
\sb160Merci pour votre courriel, et nous apprécions votre patience. Ces renseignements sont fournis à titre d'orientation générale et ne constituent pas une directive pour des dossiers individuels. Pour des demandes de renseignements sur des cas spécifiques, les demandeurs peuvent contacter le Ministère en soumettant le Formulaire Web d'IRCC. Veuillez trouver les réponses à vos questions ci-dessous :
Question 1
Je souhaiterais savoir si ce critère s'applique également aux codes de dispense d'EIMT et CAQ sous l’article R204a) pour les accords internationaux, par exemple le code T44 (personne mutée à l'intérieur d'une entreprise sous l'Accord économique et commercial global (AECG) entre le Canada et l’Union européenne).
Réponse 1
L'exigence selon laquelle l'entreprise étrangère doit être celle d'une multinationale existante ne s'applique qu'aux applications TIC spécifiquement codées C61 en vertu du R205(a).
Les demandes soumises en vertu du R204(a), bien que similaires, reflètent des engagements réciproques plus larges pris avec des partenaires commerciaux et impliquent donc certaines variations dans l'application.
L'attente en vertu du R204(a) est que l'entreprise puisse devenir une multinationale en établissant une succursale, une filiale ou une entreprise affiliée au Canada.
Question 2
La deuxième question concerne les dispenses C62 et C63. Si une entreprise a déjà été établie au Canada avant l’entrée en vigueur de la nouvelle exigence et qu’elle est active et génère déjà des revenus au Canada, doit-elle quand même répondre à cette nouvelle exigence d’être une multinationale ?
Réponse 2
Les dispositions relatives aux TIC spécifiées aux termes des C62 et C63 autorisent l'émission de WP TIC si l'une des opérations commerciales existantes est déjà établie au Canada, répondant ainsi à la définition d'une multinationale.
Nous reconnaissons que les récentes mises à jour des lignes directrices ont pu soulever des questions, et d'autres révisions sont en cours pour apporter des éclaircissements supplémentaires à ce sujet.
and Cizenship Canadaot Cioyenneté Canada
Nous espérons que ces informations vous seront utiles.
Pour plus d’informations, veuillez consulter la page Web suivante :
Personnes mutées à l'intérieur d'une société (PMIS) – ACEUM [R204a) – T37. T38] – Accords ou ententes – Programme de mobilité internationale-Canada.ca
Cordialement,
\sb160 Addresse courriel pour les représentants à l'immigration
De : Envoyé : 2 décembre 2024 16:16 À : Objet : Personnes mutées à l’intérieur d’une société (PMIS) – AECG [R204a) – T44
Madame, Monsieur,
Suite aux changements des critères d'admissibilité pour la dispense d'EIMT sous l'article R205 a) - C61, C62 et C63 (personne mutée à l'intérieur d'une compagnie), le programme exige désormais que l'entreprise soit une multinationale, c'est-à-dire une entreprise qui exerce des activités opérationnelles dans au moins un pays autre que son pays d’origine et génère des revenus au- delà de ses frontières dans au moins deux pays avant d’établir une entreprise au Canada.
Question 1 : Je souhaiterais savoir si ce critère s'applique également aux codes de dispense d'EIMT et CAQ sous l’article R204a) pour les accords internationaux, par exemple le code T44 (personne mutée à l'intérieur d'une entreprise sous l'Accord économique et commercial global (AECG) entre le Canada et l’Union européenne). Je constate que le site officiel a été mis à jour le 3 octobre, date d’entrée en vigueur de la nouvelle politique, mais il ne mentionne pas l’obligation que l’entreprise soit une multinationale.
Malheureusement, nos recherches n'ont pas permis de clarifier ce détail. Je tiens à croire que cette nouvelle exigence ne s’applique pas aux accords internationaux pour deux raisons :
- Premièrement, pour la dispense T44 (et tous les autres accords), le site ne mentionne pas que l'entreprise doit être une
and Citizenshi Canada et Ciloyeneé Canada
multinationale.
- Deuxièmement, selon ma compréhension, avant d'apporter ces changements dans les accords, le Canada devrait renégocier ces détails avec chaque pays séparément.
Question 2 : La deuxième question concerne les dispenses C62 et C63. Si une entreprise a déjà été établie au Canada avant l’entrée en vigueur de la nouvelle exigence et qu’elle est active et génère déjà des revenus au Canada, doit-elle quand même répondre à cette nouvelle exigence d’être une multinationale ? Cette question concerne également les accords internationaux.
Dans l’affirmatif, quelles options proposez-vous pour les entreprises (non pas pour les entrepreneurs) qui souhaitent s’établir au Canada mais qui ne répondent pas à l’exigence d’être une multinationale ?

Please note that this mailbox is intended for general guidance and does not provide responses to case-specific inquiries. If you have case specific questions about a file, you are encouraged to submit a Webform at: http//www.ircc.canada.ca/english/contacts/web-form.asp

\f0Question
I would like to ask about the legal status for students who are required to discontinue or RTD (also referred as “required to withdraw" at other DLIs). At our institution, student who do not meet academic progress expectation will be required to discontinue and cannot be re-admitted to any of our program for at least one academic term (usually 4 months). At the CBIE conference, it was discussed that such discontinuation is considered as authorized leave by IRCC. I would like to confirm correctness ofthe information that RTD, if instituted by DLI is considered as authorized leave.
If RTD is considered authorized leave by IRCC, we assume the following PDI section applies: [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-) manuals/temporary-residents/study-permnits/assessing-conditions.htnl#leave
D. Leave from studies Students may be required or may wish to take leave from their studies while in Canada. For the purpose of assessing if a student is actively pursuing their studies, any leave taken from a program of studies in Canada should not exceed 150 days from the date the leave commenced and must be authorized by their DLI. A student on leave who begins or resumes their studies within 150 days from the date the leave commenced (that is, the date the leave was granted by the institution) is considered to be actively pursuing studies during their leave. If a student does not resume their studies within 150 days, they should do either of the following:
- change their status (that is, change to visitor status or worker status)
- leave Canada
If they do not change their status or leave Canada, they are considered non-compliant with their study permit conditions. In cases where a student has taken multiple periods of leave in Canada during their program of study, the officer should consider the student's reasons for the various periods of leave. If the multiple periods of leave do not appear to support the expectation that the student is making reasonable progress toward the completion of their course or program of study in the time allotted by the course or program of study, the officer may determine that the study permit holder has not fulfilled the condition to actively
mmigration, Refugees pursue their course or program of study.
Examples of reasons for leave include but are not limited to the following:
- medical illness or injury
- pregnancy
- family emergency
- death or serious illness of a family member
- change in program of study within the same institution, outside a regularly scheduled break
- dismissals or suspensions (dependent on degree of severity)
- postponed program start date (see Deferred enrolment for more information)
I would like to confirm impact on legal status for students while on RTD. The recent updates of R222(1) and (a.1), stated study permit becomes invalid 90 days after the permit holder completes their studies or the day on which the permit holder is no longer enrolled at the DLI that is named in the permit.
Since a student on RTD status cannot be enrolled with us during an RTD period, does this mean their study permit becomes invalid the day they are notified of withdrawal from their program? Or will the authorized leave will provide them a status of up to 150 days. Meaning they are not required change their status (that is, change to visitor status or worker status) or leave Canada if they will resume studies at our DLI within 150 days.
Answer
Students may, in exceptional circumstances, may take a leave from their studies. The student must resume classes within 150 days of the date on which they stopped studying. There are various examples of reasons listed on the IRCC website include illness or injury, pregnancy, family emergency, death or serious illness of a family member etc. As ofNovember 8, 2024, IRCC compliance reports are mandatory where the DLI must select the appropriate student's academic status at the DLI. IRCC’s website provides several enrollment status options such as leave of absence, deferred enrollment, academic suspension, no longer registered etc. We ask you that you carefully review each definition.
You may find additional information about students who are required to discontinue or a“ required to withdraw" on the IRCC website:
1)Academic suspension The student is suspended from your institution, due to poor academic performance or violation of the institution's policies. The student is allowed to return after the period of suspension. Any leave from a program of studies in Canada should not exceed 150 consecutive days from the date the leave started. If a student exceeds 150 days of leave from studies, they will need to change their status with IRCC or will be considered non-compliant with their study permit conditions. Please note that an academic suspension is different than being no longer registered.
2)No longer registered or enrolled Your institution sent the student a letter of admission, but they are no longer registered or enrolled because they have
- been dismissed
- withdrawn voluntarily
- transferred to another institution
This status should not be used for students who are academically suspended.
- 222 (1) A study permit becomes invalid upon the first to occur of the following days:
- (a.1) the day on which the permit holder is no longer enrolled at the designated learning institution that is named in the permit, other than as a result of completing their studies;
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

- The expiry date of a TRV is the date by which the visa must be used to arrive at the port of entry (POE) and seek admission to Canada. The expiry date is not the suggested duration of the visit. A TRV does not guarantee entry to Canada, nor does it grant temporary resident status in Canada.

threads.subject: R186(l) co-op wp exemption question-REP-2024-2610 - Due 13-Jan-25
threads.answer:
Good day,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Repres entatives Mailbox
Please note that this mailbox is intended for general guidance and does not provide responses to case-specific inquiries. If you have case specific questions about a file, you are encouraged to submit a Webform at: [http://www.ircc.canada.ca/english/contacts/web-form.asp](http://www.ircc.canada.ca/english/contacts/web-form.asp)
In order to work without a work permit pursuant to paragraph R186(1), this authority must be printed on their permit.
Otherwise, exemption code C32 (co-op for post-secondary international students), intended for foreign nationals who intend to perform work that is an essential part of a post-secondary academic, vocational or professional training program offered by a designated learning institution (DLI) in Canada would apply. The work cannot form more than 50% of the total program of study.
The acceptance letter provided by the DLI should clearly establish that the work is an essential part ofthe academic, vocational or professional training program that all participants enrolled in the program are required to complete in order to receive their degree, diploma or certificate. The most common example is undergraduate co-op programs at universities and colleges. If an unpaid internship or other activity for work experience is required to obtain the credits needed for graduation, an international student is required to apply and obtain a co-op work permit.
\cbpat4Students who are already in Canada and have applied for a co-op work permit may begin their co-op placement using their on-campus and off-campus work authorization, provided they meet all the eligibility requirements. There is no limit on work hours for on-campus work. A student may accept employment on the campus of the university or college at which they are a full-time student under paragraph 186(f).
\cbpat4\sb173For off-campus work authorization, as per paragraph R186(v), students can work a total of 24 hours per week during an academic term or semester while they are waiting for their co-op work permit; however, the 24 hours must include both the hours worked at their co-op job and those worked at their regular paid job (if they have one). They can work full-time during the regularly scheduled breaks.
\cbpat4\sb173If the co-op work permit application is refused, they must stop their co-op work immediately.
\sb173For more information, please see: Work related to a research, educational or training program– exemption codes C31, C32 and C33 (International Mobility Program) - Canada.ca
\sb240Thank you,
